domains.title: System Design
domains.short_overview: How to design software systems that meet real functional and non-functional requirements under real constraints — from a single request's network path through to production deployment and reliability.

children.title: Requirements
children.short_overview: What a system must do, how well, and under what constraints — decided before any design work starts.

children.title: Functional Requirements
children.short_overview: What the system must actually do — the observable behaviors a user or another system can call and depend on (e.g. 'POST /customers creates a customer').

sections.what: What the system must actually do — the observable behaviors a user or another system can call and depend on (e.g. 'POST /customers creates a customer').
sections.how: Captured as concrete, testable statements, not vague goals. This project's CustomerController endpoints are its functional requirements made real.

children.title: Non-Functional Requirements
children.short_overview: Quality attributes a system must have regardless of specific feature: latency, availability, security, cost, observability — the 'how well', not the 'what'.

sections.what: Quality attributes a system must have regardless of specific feature: latency, availability, security, cost, observability — the 'how well', not the 'what'.
sections.how: Stated as measurable targets (e.g. p99 latency, uptime %) so they can be tested, not left as adjectives like 'fast' or 'scalable'.

children.title: Scale
children.short_overview: The expected volume (requests/sec, data size, concurrent users) a design must handle — determines whether a simple design suffices or a more complex one is justified.

sections.what: The expected volume (requests/sec, data size, concurrent users) a design must handle — determines whether a simple design suffices or a more complex one is justified.
sections.how: Estimate real numbers before designing (back-of-envelope: requests/day / seconds/day = avg QPS, plus a peak multiplier) rather than assuming 'web scale' by default.

children.title: Constraints
children.short_overview: Fixed boundaries a design must work within — budget, team size, existing infrastructure, compliance, deadline — that are not requirements but shape which requirements are even achievable.

sections.what: Fixed boundaries a design must work within — budget, team size, existing infrastructure, compliance, deadline — that are not requirements but shape which requirements are even achievable.
sections.how: This project's own constraints (single-operator budget, no paid infra beyond Railway/Vercel free-ish tiers, no enterprise identity provider) directly shaped its architecture (H2 in-memory DB instead of managed Postgres for the Customer app, no auth layer yet).

children.title: SLO/SLA Concepts
children.short_overview: SLI (a measured indicator, e.g. latency) -> SLO (an internal target for that indicator) -> SLA (an external, often contractual, commitment built on an SLO).

sections.what: SLI (a measured indicator, e.g. latency) -> SLO (an internal target for that indicator) -> SLA (an external, often contractual, commitment built on an SLO).

children.title: Acceptance Criteria
children.short_overview: The explicit, checkable conditions that decide whether a requirement is actually satisfied — the bridge between 'what we want' and 'can we prove it's done'.

sections.what: The explicit, checkable conditions that decide whether a requirement is actually satisfied — the bridge between 'what we want' and 'can we prove it's done'.
sections.how: This project's own Acceptance Contract (agent/acceptance_contract.py) formalizes exactly this idea for AI-driven changes: requirement_id, expected_observable_effect, required_gates, allowed_terminal_outcomes.

children.title: APIs
children.short_overview: The contracts through which independently-deployed systems (or a frontend and backend) communicate.

children.title: REST
children.short_overview: An architectural style using HTTP verbs (GET/POST/PUT/DELETE) over resource-shaped URLs, with each request self-contained (stateless).

sections.what: An architectural style using HTTP verbs (GET/POST/PUT/DELETE) over resource-shaped URLs, with each request self-contained (stateless).
sections.how: This project's Customer app exposes REST endpoints (GET /customers/{id}, POST /customers) using Spring Boot's @RestController.

children.title: GraphQL
children.short_overview: A query language letting a client request exactly the fields it needs in one round trip, resolved server-side by field-level resolvers instead of fixed endpoint shapes.

sections.what: A query language letting a client request exactly the fields it needs in one round trip, resolved server-side by field-level resolvers instead of fixed endpoint shapes.
sections.how: Trades REST's simple caching/tooling for flexible, precise queries — better suited when clients have very different data needs (e.g. mobile vs. web) than when one shape serves everyone.

children.title: Contracts
children.short_overview: An explicit, versioned agreement (types, required/optional fields, error shapes) between an API and its callers, checked mechanically rather than left as a mutual assumption.

sections.what: An explicit, versioned agreement (types, required/optional fields, error shapes) between an API and its callers, checked mechanically rather than left as a mutual assumption.

children.title: Validation
children.short_overview: Rejecting a malformed or unsafe request before it reaches business logic, with a clear error rather than a confusing downstream failure.

sections.what: Rejecting a malformed or unsafe request before it reaches business logic, with a clear error rather than a confusing downstream failure.
sections.how: This project's Customer entity uses Jakarta Bean Validation (spring-boot-starter-validation) to reject invalid input at the boundary.

children.title: Versioning
children.short_overview: How an API evolves without breaking existing callers — via URL path (/v2/...), header, or strictly-additive changes only.

sections.what: How an API evolves without breaking existing callers — via URL path (/v2/...), header, or strictly-additive changes only.

children.title: Idempotency
children.short_overview: A request that can be safely retried without causing a second effect — critical for any client that might resend a request after a timeout (was it applied or not?).

sections.what: A request that can be safely retried without causing a second effect — critical for any client that might resend a request after a timeout (was it applied or not?).
sections.how: Typically implemented via a client-supplied idempotency key the server deduplicates on, or by designing the operation itself to be naturally repeatable (e.g. 'set X to 5' vs. 'add 5 to X').

children.title: Error Handling
children.short_overview: Returning a specific, actionable error (status code + machine-readable reason) instead of a generic failure, so a caller (human or another system) can react correctly.

sections.what: Returning a specific, actionable error (status code + machine-readable reason) instead of a generic failure, so a caller (human or another system) can react correctly.
sections.how: This project's own qa-evaluator explicitly requires a specific failure reason to reach the caller (e.g. RepoToolError re-raised as MCP's ToolError) rather than a generic message — the same principle applied to AI tool design as to API design.

children.title: Networking
children.short_overview: The layers a request travels through between a client and a server, and where each kind of failure/latency actually happens.

children.title: DNS
children.short_overview: Translates a hostname (e.g. agentic-platform-backend-production.up.railway.app) into an IP address before any connection can be made — the first, often-overlooked point of failure or latency.

sections.what: Translates a hostname (e.g. agentic-platform-backend-production.up.railway.app) into an IP address before any connection can be made — the first, often-overlooked point of failure or latency.
sections.how: This project hit a real DNS failure: a Cloudflare Quick Tunnel registered successfully at the edge but its hostname never resolved in public DNS — confirmed via direct queries to Cloudflare's own resolver, not guessed.

children.title: TCP
children.short_overview: A reliable, ordered, connection-oriented transport protocol underlying HTTP — establishes a connection (three-way handshake) before any data flows.

sections.what: A reliable, ordered, connection-oriented transport protocol underlying HTTP — establishes a connection (three-way handshake) before any data flows.

children.title: TLS
children.short_overview: Encrypts and authenticates a connection (the 'S' in HTTPS) using a certificate proving the server's identity — a custom domain isn't fully live until its own certificate is provisioned.

sections.what: Encrypts and authenticates a connection (the 'S' in HTTPS) using a certificate proving the server's identity — a custom domain isn't fully live until its own certificate is provisioned.
sections.how: This project's custom domain (agentic.karthikdevadoss.com) had its DNS configured but certificate provisioning was still pending — directly observed via a real TLS handshake failure (SEC_E_WRONG_PRINCIPAL), not assumed.

children.title: HTTP
children.short_overview: The application-layer protocol (request/response, methods, status codes, headers) almost all web APIs are built on.

sections.what: The application-layer protocol (request/response, methods, status codes, headers) almost all web APIs are built on.
sections.how: Every route in this project's own Starlette backend (agent/web_server.py) and Spring Boot Customer app is an HTTP handler.

children.title: Proxy
children.short_overview: An intermediary that forwards requests on behalf of a client or server — used for caching, load balancing, TLS termination, or reaching a network the client can't reach directly.

sections.what: An intermediary that forwards requests on behalf of a client or server — used for caching, load balancing, TLS termination, or reaching a network the client can't reach directly.
sections.how: This project reached its own event-ledger Postgres instance over a public TCP proxy (Railway's private DATABASE_URL isn't reachable from a laptop), and Cloudflare/ngrok tunnels were used as reverse proxies for temporary public access.

children.title: Load Balancer
children.short_overview: Distributes incoming requests across multiple server instances for capacity and fault tolerance — not currently needed at this project's single-instance scale.

sections.what: Distributes incoming requests across multiple server instances for capacity and fault tolerance — not currently needed at this project's single-instance scale.

children.title: Timeout
children.short_overview: An explicit limit on how long to wait for a response before giving up — without one, a hung dependency can hang every caller indefinitely.

sections.what: An explicit limit on how long to wait for a response before giving up — without one, a hung dependency can hang every caller indefinitely.
sections.how: This project found a real bug where the Target Application panel could load forever because fetch() has no built-in timeout — fixed with an explicit Promise.race 8-second timeout.

children.title: Retry
children.short_overview: Re-attempting a failed request, usually with backoff, when the failure is likely transient — must be paired with idempotency to be safe.

sections.what: Re-attempting a failed request, usually with backoff, when the failure is likely transient — must be paired with idempotency to be safe.
sections.how: This project's event ledger retries a failed remote insert via a local outage spool with idempotent (ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING) retry, so a retry can never create a duplicate row.

children.title: Compute
children.short_overview: The runtime resources (processes, threads, CPU, memory) a program actually executes on.

children.title: Process
children.short_overview: An OS-level unit of execution with its own memory space — this project's Spring Boot app and its Python agent run as separate processes.

sections.what: An OS-level unit of execution with its own memory space — this project's Spring Boot app and its Python agent run as separate processes.

children.title: Thread
children.short_overview: A unit of execution within a process, sharing its memory — Spring Boot's embedded Tomcat handles each HTTP request on its own thread by default.

sections.what: A unit of execution within a process, sharing its memory — Spring Boot's embedded Tomcat handles each HTTP request on its own thread by default.

children.title: CPU
children.short_overview: The physical resource actually executing instructions — a bottleneck when work is computation-heavy (e.g. embedding generation) rather than I/O-bound.

sections.what: The physical resource actually executing instructions — a bottleneck when work is computation-heavy (e.g. embedding generation) rather than I/O-bound.

children.title: Memory
children.short_overview: RAM available to a process — a JVM's heap size, or a Python process's working set, both bounded by real memory the host actually has.

sections.what: RAM available to a process — a JVM's heap size, or a Python process's working set, both bounded by real memory the host actually has.

children.title: JVM
children.short_overview: The Java Virtual Machine — compiles Java bytecode to native execution, manages memory (heap/garbage collection) and threading for this project's Spring Boot Customer app.

sections.what: The Java Virtual Machine — compiles Java bytecode to native execution, manages memory (heap/garbage collection) and threading for this project's Spring Boot Customer app.
sections.how: This project's app/ directory is a real Spring Boot 4.1.1 / Java 17 application running on a real JVM, compiled and tested via Maven (mvnw).

children.title: Concurrency
children.short_overview: Multiple logical tasks making progress over the same time period — via threads, async I/O, or separate processes — each with different tradeoffs for shared-state safety.

sections.what: Multiple logical tasks making progress over the same time period — via threads, async I/O, or separate processes — each with different tradeoffs for shared-state safety.
sections.how: This project's Starlette backend uses async request handlers plus background threads (for run execution) and a lock-guarded background sync trigger for the event ledger spool, to avoid blocking the fast synchronous telemetry path.

children.title: Databases
children.short_overview: Systems of record for persistent, structured data — how it's stored, queried, and kept consistent.

children.title: Relational DB
children.short_overview: Stores data in tables with defined schemas and relationships, queried via SQL — this project uses H2 (in-memory, for the Customer app demo) and Postgres (durable, for the event ledger).

sections.what: Stores data in tables with defined schemas and relationships, queried via SQL — this project uses H2 (in-memory, for the Customer app demo) and Postgres (durable, for the event ledger).

children.title: Oracle
children.short_overview: A widely-used enterprise relational database — not used anywhere in this project's own code; general knowledge only.

sections.what: A widely-used enterprise relational database — not used anywhere in this project's own code; general knowledge only.

children.title: JDBC
children.short_overview: Java's standard low-level API for connecting to and querying a relational database — JPA is built on top of it.

sections.what: Java's standard low-level API for connecting to and querying a relational database — JPA is built on top of it.
sections.how: Spring Data JPA (used by this project's Customer app) uses JDBC underneath via Hibernate.

children.title: JPA
children.short_overview: Java Persistence API — an ORM standard mapping Java objects to relational rows, implemented here by Hibernate via Spring Data JPA.

sections.what: Java Persistence API — an ORM standard mapping Java objects to relational rows, implemented here by Hibernate via Spring Data JPA.
sections.how: This project's Customer entity/CustomerRepository use Spring Data JPA directly.

children.title: Transactions
children.short_overview: A group of database operations that either all succeed or all roll back together (ACID) — prevents a partial, inconsistent write from ever being visible.

sections.what: A group of database operations that either all succeed or all roll back together (ACID) — prevents a partial, inconsistent write from ever being visible.

children.title: Indexing
children.short_overview: A data structure (typically a B-tree) letting the database find rows without scanning the whole table — the standard fix for a slow query on a large table.

sections.what: A data structure (typically a B-tree) letting the database find rows without scanning the whole table — the standard fix for a slow query on a large table.

children.title: Connection Pooling
children.short_overview: Reuses a fixed set of already-open database connections across requests instead of opening/closing one per request — opening a real DB connection is expensive.

sections.what: Reuses a fixed set of already-open database connections across requests instead of opening/closing one per request — opening a real DB connection is expensive.
sections.how: Spring Boot defaults to HikariCP as its connection pool whenever spring-boot-starter-data-jpa is on the classpath, as it is in this project's Customer app, even without explicit pool configuration.

children.title: Replication
children.short_overview: Copying a database's data to one or more additional nodes for read scaling and/or failover — not used in this project's current single-instance setup.

sections.what: Copying a database's data to one or more additional nodes for read scaling and/or failover — not used in this project's current single-instance setup.

children.title: Partitioning
children.short_overview: Splitting a large table's data across multiple physical segments (by range, hash, etc.) so no single segment grows unbounded — a scale technique this project's current data volume doesn't yet need.

sections.what: Splitting a large table's data across multiple physical segments (by range, hash, etc.) so no single segment grows unbounded — a scale technique this project's current data volume doesn't yet need.

children.title: Caching
children.short_overview: Storing a cheap-to-read copy of expensive-to-compute or expensive-to-fetch data, at the cost of it potentially going stale.

children.title: Redis
children.short_overview: An in-memory key-value store commonly used for caching, sessions, and pub/sub — not used anywhere in this project's own code; general knowledge only.

sections.what: An in-memory key-value store commonly used for caching, sessions, and pub/sub — not used anywhere in this project's own code; general knowledge only.

children.title: Cache-Aside
children.short_overview: The application checks the cache first; on a miss, it reads the real source, then populates the cache for next time — the most common caching pattern.

sections.what: The application checks the cache first; on a miss, it reads the real source, then populates the cache for next time — the most common caching pattern.

children.title: TTL
children.short_overview: Time-to-live — an expiration after which a cached value is considered stale and must be refreshed, bounding how wrong a cache can be.

sections.what: Time-to-live — an expiration after which a cached value is considered stale and must be refreshed, bounding how wrong a cache can be.

children.title: Invalidation
children.short_overview: Actively removing/updating a cached value the moment its source changes, rather than waiting for TTL expiry — famously one of the two hard problems in computer science.

sections.what: Actively removing/updating a cached value the moment its source changes, rather than waiting for TTL expiry — famously one of the two hard problems in computer science.
sections.how: This project's own PDF book cache (learn_pdf.py) invalidates by content hash of the canonical Learn tree rather than a fixed TTL, so a stale book is never served after Learn content genuinely changes.

children.title: Consistency
children.short_overview: How quickly and reliably a cache's value matches its underlying source of truth after a write — a real tradeoff against caching's whole performance benefit.

sections.what: How quickly and reliably a cache's value matches its underlying source of truth after a write — a real tradeoff against caching's whole performance benefit.

children.title: Distributed Systems
children.short_overview: Systems whose components run on separate machines/processes and communicate over an unreliable network — different failure assumptions than a single process.

children.title: Availability
children.short_overview: The fraction of time a system successfully responds to requests — often traded against consistency under network partition (CAP theorem).

sections.what: The fraction of time a system successfully responds to requests — often traded against consistency under network partition (CAP theorem).

children.title: Consistency
children.short_overview: Whether every reader sees the same (and most recent) data at the same time — strong consistency is expensive across a network; many real systems choose eventual consistency deliberately.

sections.what: Whether every reader sees the same (and most recent) data at the same time — strong consistency is expensive across a network; many real systems choose eventual consistency deliberately.

children.title: Retry
children.short_overview: See System Design -> Networking -> Retry — the same idempotency-paired principle applies across service boundaries.

sections.what: See System Design -> Networking -> Retry — the same idempotency-paired principle applies across service boundaries.

children.title: Idempotency
children.short_overview: See System Design -> APIs -> Idempotency — critical at scale, since network partitions make 'did that request actually land?' a routine question, not an edge case.

sections.what: See System Design -> APIs -> Idempotency — critical at scale, since network partitions make 'did that request actually land?' a routine question, not an edge case.

children.title: Queues
children.short_overview: A durable buffer decoupling a producer from a consumer, so the consumer can process work at its own pace and survive being temporarily down.

sections.what: A durable buffer decoupling a producer from a consumer, so the consumer can process work at its own pace and survive being temporarily down.

children.title: Kafka
children.short_overview: A distributed, partitioned, replicated log used as a high-throughput event streaming/queueing backbone — not used anywhere in this project's own code; general knowledge only.

sections.what: A distributed, partitioned, replicated log used as a high-throughput event streaming/queueing backbone — not used anywhere in this project's own code; general knowledge only.

children.title: Event-Driven Architecture
children.short_overview: Components react to events (facts that already happened) rather than being directly called — this project's own event ledger is a lightweight, single-table instance of the same core idea (append-only, consumers read from it independently).

sections.what: Components react to events (facts that already happened) rather than being directly called — this project's own event ledger is a lightweight, single-table instance of the same core idea (append-only, consumers read from it independently).
sections.how: agent/event_ledger.py's delivery_events table is an append-only log every part of this platform (Dashboard, Usage, Learn's knowledge-candidate pipeline) reads from independently, rather than services calling each other directly.

children.title: Security
children.short_overview: Protecting a system's data, identity, and actions from unauthorized access or use.

children.title: Authentication
children.short_overview: Verifying who is making a request (login, tokens, API keys) — not yet implemented anywhere in this project's own Customer app (explicitly out of scope so far).

sections.what: Verifying who is making a request (login, tokens, API keys) — not yet implemented anywhere in this project's own Customer app (explicitly out of scope so far).

children.title: Authorization
children.short_overview: Deciding what an already-authenticated identity is allowed to do — distinct from authentication, and the concept this project's risk_policy.py applies to AI actions rather than human identities (what is this agent allowed to auto-execute).

sections.what: Deciding what an already-authenticated identity is allowed to do — distinct from authentication, and the concept this project's risk_policy.py applies to AI actions rather than human identities (what is this agent allowed to auto-execute).
sections.how: agent/risk_policy.py deterministically gates auto-execution by risk/complexity, structurally separate from the reasoning it gates — the same 'authorization is a separate deterministic decision' principle as classic app authorization.

children.title: JWT
children.short_overview: A signed, self-contained token (JSON Web Token) commonly used to carry identity/claims between services without a shared session store — not used anywhere in this project's own code; general knowledge only.

sections.what: A signed, self-contained token (JSON Web Token) commonly used to carry identity/claims between services without a shared session store — not used anywhere in this project's own code; general knowledge only.

children.title: Spring Security
children.short_overview: Spring's authentication/authorization framework — not used in this project's Customer app (no auth layer implemented yet); general knowledge only.

sections.what: Spring's authentication/authorization framework — not used in this project's Customer app (no auth layer implemented yet); general knowledge only.

children.title: Cognito
children.short_overview: AWS's managed identity/user-pool service — not used anywhere in this project; general knowledge only.

sections.what: AWS's managed identity/user-pool service — not used anywhere in this project; general knowledge only.

children.title: FusionAuth
children.short_overview: A self-hostable identity/auth server — not used anywhere in this project; general knowledge only.

sections.what: A self-hostable identity/auth server — not used anywhere in this project; general knowledge only.

children.title: Secrets
children.short_overview: Credentials/keys that must never be committed, logged, or exposed to a model's output — this project actively enforces this (redact_secrets(), .env gitignored, key rotation after one real exposure).

sections.what: Credentials/keys that must never be committed, logged, or exposed to a model's output — this project actively enforces this (redact_secrets(), .env gitignored, key rotation after one real exposure).
sections.how: tools.redact_secrets() deterministically redacts credential-shaped values before anything reaches a log, trace, or the event ledger — applied at the shared boundary so every consumer benefits automatically.

children.title: Least Privilege
children.short_overview: Granting only the access actually needed for a task, nothing more — this project's qa-evaluator subagent is a direct application: Read/Glob/Grep/Bash/WebFetch only, Write/Edit explicitly disallowed.

sections.what: Granting only the access actually needed for a task, nothing more — this project's qa-evaluator subagent is a direct application: Read/Glob/Grep/Bash/WebFetch only, Write/Edit explicitly disallowed.
sections.how: `.claude/agents/qa-evaluator.md`'s disallowedTools (Write/Edit/NotebookEdit) enforces least privilege structurally for an AI subagent, the same principle as scoping a service account's IAM permissions.

children.title: Reliability
children.short_overview: Keeping a system correct and available in the presence of real failures, not just under ideal conditions.

children.title: Failure Modes
children.short_overview: The specific, enumerable ways a system can go wrong — naming them explicitly (timeout vs. crash vs. wrong-data vs. partial-success) is what makes them detectable and preventable rather than a vague 'something broke'.

sections.what: The specific, enumerable ways a system can go wrong — naming them explicitly (timeout vs. crash vs. wrong-data vs. partial-success) is what makes them detectable and preventable rather than a vague 'something broke'.

children.title: Retry
children.short_overview: See Networking -> Retry.

sections.what: See Networking -> Retry.

children.title: Timeout
children.short_overview: See Networking -> Timeout.

sections.what: See Networking -> Timeout.

children.title: Circuit Breaker
children.short_overview: Stops calling a dependency that's already failing repeatedly, for a cooldown period, instead of piling up more failing/slow calls on top of an already-struggling system.

sections.what: Stops calling a dependency that's already failing repeatedly, for a cooldown period, instead of piling up more failing/slow calls on top of an already-struggling system.

children.title: Requested-Effect Verification (Production Verification)
children.short_overview: The practice of confirming a deployed change's SPECIFIC requested observable effect is genuinely live in production — not merely that a server responds, or that a deploy command exited 0.

sections.what: The practice of confirming a deployed change's SPECIFIC requested observable effect is genuinely live in production — not merely that a server responds, or that a deploy command exited 0.
sections.why: HTTP 200 and 'deployment succeeded' both prove the server is reachable, not that the requested content is there. Skipping this step is exactly how a false success gets reported to a human.
sections.how: Capture the exact expected new content (e.g. the literal new file bytes) before deploying. After the deploy is believed active, independently fetch the real production endpoint and compare against that captured expectation — not a paraphrase, not a status code. Only mark the change COMPLETED/verified when the comparison matches.
sections.when: Any time a system deploys or applies a change autonomously and needs to report success/failure to a human or another system. Unnecessary for read-only investigation with no mutation.
sections.real_experience: Real incident: Workbench run trainer-7769757e reported 'Deployment: VERIFIED (HTTP 200)' and claimed a footer changed to requested text, but the real Customer App still showed the OLD footer — the deploy-wait loop had exited early on a Railway CLI 'Online' signal that actually described the PREVIOUS deployment still serving traffic while the new one built in the background. Fixed in agent/web_server.py::_decide_deployment_outcome and the VERIFYING PRODUCTION polling loop: production is now polled directly for the exact expected content (agent/web_server.py's run.trainer_expected_content) for up to 15 minutes, and COMPLETED requires BOTH reachability AND content match.
development_steps: Observed: Workbench UI showed VERIFIED but real production had old content.
Investigated event ledger for the real run (never guessed) — found content_changed_from_baseline=false was captured but unused by the decision function.
Root-caused the deploy-wait loop's premature exit on a Railway CLI text signal that doesn't distinguish OLD-still-serving from NEW-active.
Fixed _decide_deployment_outcome to require content_verified, not just HTTP 200.
Added regression tests reproducing the exact false-positive scenario.
Re-verified live with a real public acceptance run.
failure_modes: A CLI status text ('Online') can describe a stale deployment, not the one you just triggered.
Never treat 'the deploy command succeeded' as equivalent to 'the change is live'.

interview.question: How do you know a deployment actually worked?
interview.short_answer: Never trust HTTP 200 or a CLI exit code alone — independently fetch the real endpoint and check for the specific content you expected to change.
interview.deep_answer: Deployment transport success (the server is reachable, the deploy command exited 0) is a different claim from software-change success (the requested behavior is actually live). We had a real incident where a Workbench run reported 'VERIFIED' based on HTTP 200 while the old content was still being served — root cause was a CLI status signal describing a stale, still-serving deployment. The fix: capture the exact expected new content before deploying, then independently re-fetch production and do a real comparison — never a status code — before reporting success.
interview.real_incident_story: run trainer-7769757e claimed a footer change was live; the Customer App still showed the old text. The deploy had genuinely completed in the background moments later — the bug was in when and how we checked, not in the deploy itself.

children.title: Rollback
children.short_overview: Reverting to a known-good prior version when a deployment is found to be bad — requires that prior version to actually still be deployable/available.

sections.what: Reverting to a known-good prior version when a deployment is found to be bad — requires that prior version to actually still be deployable/available.

children.title: Recovery
children.short_overview: Restoring correct operation after a failure — for data, this means a tested restore path, not just a backup that has never been proven to actually restore.

sections.what: Restoring correct operation after a failure — for data, this means a tested restore path, not just a backup that has never been proven to actually restore.
sections.how: This project's event ledger has a manual on-demand portable backup that has exported real rows successfully, but a restore has explicitly NOT yet been tested — an honestly-tracked open gap, not assumed solved.

children.title: Observability
children.short_overview: Being able to answer 'what is this system actually doing right now, and what did it just do' from real captured evidence, not from guessing.

children.title: Logs
children.short_overview: Discrete, timestamped records of what happened — this project's own safe trace (tool name, sanitized input, status) is a deliberately narrow log designed to never leak secrets or file contents.

sections.what: Discrete, timestamped records of what happened — this project's own safe trace (tool name, sanitized input, status) is a deliberately narrow log designed to never leak secrets or file contents.

children.title: Durable Append-Only Event Ledger
children.short_overview: A single canonical, append-only Postgres table capturing every observable engineering event (model calls, tool calls, proposals, approvals, builds, tests, commits, deployments, human interventions) with a stable envelope schema.

sections.what: A single canonical, append-only Postgres table capturing every observable engineering event (model calls, tool calls, proposals, approvals, builds, tests, commits, deployments, human interventions) with a stable envelope schema.
sections.why: Before this existed, every observable event lived only in one process's memory and a small local gitignored log — a crash or a lost laptop meant losing all history. Historical trajectories cannot be reconstructed after the fact if never captured.
sections.how: One table (infra/event-ledger/schema.sql), a canonical envelope (event_id, timestamp, event_type, run_id, source, activity_class, provider/model/token columns, a JSONB payload for event-specific data), write-through inserts the moment each event happens (never batched), idempotent via ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING on event_id, with a local outage spool as a fallback so an insert failure never drops an event.
sections.when: Any system where 'what actually happened, in order, with evidence' needs to survive process restarts, crashes, or feed future analysis/evals — not needed for a purely stateless, disposable computation with no need to reconstruct history.
sections.real_experience: Built as the project's declared #1 near-term priority ('durability first'). Additive design proved itself repeatedly: new event types (repository_workspace_check, run_usage_summary, and this session's v2_trial events) were added without any schema migration, just new event_type strings and JSONB payload shapes — because the schema was designed with a flexible payload column from the start.
development_steps: Chose Railway Postgres (already-trusted provider) over introducing a new datastore.
Designed one canonical envelope instead of a table per event type.
Wired write-through recording into every real event emission point.
Added an outage-safe local spool + idempotent retry.
Backfilled historical local logs with clear reconstructed-evidence tagging, never mixed with live-observed events.
failure_modes: A field only ever written into JSONB payload (never a dedicated column) is invisible to any query that selects columns directly — a real bug found this session when run_usage_summary's real cost data wasn't reaching a dashboard that queried columns.

interview.question: How would you design durable observability for an agentic system?
interview.short_answer: One append-only table, one flexible envelope with a JSONB payload for event-specific fields, write-through inserts, idempotent by event_id, with an outage spool as a fallback — never batch-at-end.
interview.deep_answer: The core design decision is capturing broadly with provenance now and interpreting later — raw evidence that isn't captured at the moment it happens can never be reconstructed. One canonical envelope avoids table-per-event-type proliferation while a payload JSONB column lets new event types be added additively, with zero migrations, as long as the shape is a JSON object. Idempotent inserts (ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING on a UUID event_id) make retries after an outage safe. The real lesson from operating this: don't let a field live ONLY in the payload if a downstream query needs to select on or aggregate it directly.
interview.real_incident_story: A dashboard economics section showed 'NOT CAPTURED YET' even though real cost data existed the whole time in run_usage_summary events — because that data lived only inside the JSONB payload, and the dashboard's hardcoded display never queried the ledger at all. Root cause was two bugs stacked: a stale hardcoded UI plus a real column-vs-payload gap.

children.title: Acceptance Contracts (Define Success Before Coding)
children.short_overview: A small, machine-readable definition of what 'done' means for a change — requirement, target, expected observable effect, required deterministic gates, allowed terminal outcomes — captured BEFORE any implementation starts.

sections.what: A small, machine-readable definition of what 'done' means for a change — requirement, target, expected observable effect, required deterministic gates, allowed terminal outcomes — captured BEFORE any implementation starts.
sections.why: Without an explicit contract, 'did this work?' gets answered by whoever implemented it, using whatever criteria occur to them after the fact — exactly the condition that produces false-success reports.
sections.how: A small schema (agent/acceptance_contract.py: requirement_id, requirement_text, target_application, expected_observable_effect, required_gates, allowed_terminal_outcomes, evidence_requirements) with a validate() that rejects a contract whose success criterion isn't independently checkable, and cross-checks that referenced gates/outcomes are real things the runtime can actually produce.
sections.when: Any autonomous or semi-autonomous change where success needs to be judged by someone/something other than the implementer. Overkill for a one-line change a human reviews directly with full context.
sections.real_experience: Designed and standalone-tested (agent/test_acceptance_contract.py, 7/7 passing) — not yet wired into the live Workbench pipeline. Used for real in both V2 shadow trials: each trial's contract explicitly required an EXACT expected string, which is precisely what let Trial #2's evaluator catch a one-character seeded defect.
development_steps: Identified the false-success incident as a symptom of undefined success criteria.
Designed the smallest useful schema, not a general workflow engine.
Added a validate() that checks the contract itself for a checkable success criterion.
Cross-checked allowed_terminal_outcomes against the real runtime's TERMINAL_RUN_STATES via a test — proving the two can never silently drift apart.

interview.question: How do you prevent an AI agent from grading its own homework?
interview.short_answer: Write down exactly what 'done' means, in a checkable form, before the agent starts — then have someone/something else check the real evidence against that definition, not the agent's own report.
interview.deep_answer: An Acceptance Contract makes the success criterion an artifact that exists independently of the implementation, created before any code is written. The critical design point is that the contract's own validator rejects vague or unverifiable success criteria — a requirement like 'the page looks better' isn't acceptable; 'the response contains this exact string' is. This doesn't replace independent evaluation — it's the input to it.
interview.real_incident_story: In Shadow Trial #2, the contract explicitly demanded an EXACT string. A seeded one-character capitalization defect ('Find A Customer' vs the required 'Find a Customer') would have been easy to wave away as 'close enough' without that exactness requirement — the evaluator caught it precisely because the bar was unambiguous.

children.title: Independent QA Evaluation (The Implementer May Not Certify Itself)
children.short_overview: A second, genuinely separate reasoning process that checks a proposed change's real evidence against its Acceptance Contract — without access to the implementer's own claims, reasoning trace, or self-assessment.

sections.what: A second, genuinely separate reasoning process that checks a proposed change's real evidence against its Acceptance Contract — without access to the implementer's own claims, reasoning trace, or self-assessment.
sections.why: Self-evaluation by the same agent/context that did the work tends toward optimism — it already believes its own reasoning was sound. Anthropic's own harness research and this project's own real incident both point the same direction: separating generator from evaluator improves reliability, especially exactly where self-evaluation is weakest.
sections.how: A distinct subagent definition (.claude/agents/qa-evaluator.md) with restricted tools (read/test/fetch only, no Write/Edit), given ONLY the Acceptance Contract and pointers to real evidence — never told the implementer's claimed outcome. It re-runs or re-reads deterministic checks itself (re-fetch, re-compile, re-read source) rather than trusting any prior report, and returns PASS/FAIL/UNKNOWN.
sections.when: Worth the extra cost/latency when a false positive is genuinely costly (production changes, security-relevant code, anything reported to a human as fact) and the task is hard enough that self-evaluation is known to be unreliable. Not worth it for trivial, easily-human-checked changes.
sections.real_experience: Built and run three times (V2 Shadow Trials #1-#3). A real, honest limitation was found and later resolved: the custom subagent type was not recognized as a native subagent_type in two long-running sessions that predated/outlived its creation (ACT-006) — worked around transparently in Trials #1-#2 by having a general-purpose agent read and follow qa-evaluator.md verbatim, clearly labeled as not-native. A genuinely fresh Claude Code v2.1.268 session (Trial #3) confirmed native invocation works with no workaround: the subagent self-identified its role, used only its allowed tools, and returned real independently-gathered evidence. Trial #2 proved the concept concretely: the evaluator caught a deliberately seeded, subtle defect (a capitalization mismatch) with byte-exact verification. Trial #3 attempted to test a harder property — refusing to guess (UNKNOWN) under genuinely insufficient evidence — and surfaced a subtler lesson about contract design instead (see 'evaluator-uncertainty-and-verdict-design').
development_steps: Designed the subagent with an explicit 'may not certify its own production success' non-negotiable rule for the IMPLEMENTER, and a symmetric independence rule for the evaluator itself.

Trial #1: ran a correct change through the evaluator — PASS, with real independent re-verification (re-fetch, re-compile, re-read source), plus one valuable unprompted process question about commit-gating semantics.
Trial #2: seeded exactly one controlled, harmless defect after a correct implementation, withheld this from the evaluator entirely, and confirmed it returned FAIL with exact matching evidence.
ACT-006 fresh-session probe: confirmed native subagent_type='qa-evaluator' registration works with zero workaround.

Trial #3: designed a 2-criterion contract intending to elicit UNKNOWN; the evaluator instead correctly reasoned that a verifiably-absent required artifact is conclusive FAIL evidence, not an unknowable gap — a genuine, useful safety property (it never fabricated the missing evidence to force a verdict either way), even though it didn't test the originally-intended capability.
failure_modes: Native subagent definitions may not be visible to a session that was already running when the definition file was added — RESOLVED: verified fixed in a genuinely fresh session (ACT-006 closed 2026-09-11).

The evaluator's own token/cost usage is only available as an AGGREGATE_ONLY total per subagent invocation (Agent tool task-notification: total tokens/tool_uses/duration_ms) — no input/output/cache/cost decomposition is exposed by Claude Code's hook interface (verified by inspecting claude_code_hook.py's own documented hook-field list). Now at least durably recorded per actor_role in the event ledger (subagent_usage_summary events) rather than lost to conversation scrollback.

Designing a contract that reliably elicits UNKNOWN is harder than it looks — a 'required evidence is missing' criterion must be unreachable/unrulable by ANY of the evaluator's tools, not just 'the expected artifact isn't there' (see evaluator-uncertainty-and-verdict-design).

interview.question: Why not just let the same agent that made the change verify it?
interview.short_answer: Because it already believes its own reasoning — an independent evaluator with no access to the implementer's claims, checking real evidence itself, catches what self-review structurally can't.
interview.deep_answer: This mirrors an ordinary code-review principle (a reviewer shouldn't approve their own PR) applied to AI agents specifically because LLM self-evaluation has a documented tendency toward leniency. The design choices that make this actually work: (1) genuine context separation, so the evaluator never inherits the implementer's framing of the problem; (2) the evaluator re-does real checks itself instead of trusting reported results; (3) evidence requirements are defined by the Acceptance Contract in advance, so the evaluator can't quietly loosen the bar to reach a comfortable verdict.
interview.real_incident_story: In a controlled trial, we corrected a heading to 'Find a Customer', then secretly changed it to 'Find A Customer' before showing the evaluator anything. It independently fetched the live page, ran `cat -A` to check for hidden characters, and correctly reported FAIL — never told a defect existed or where.

children.title: Designing for UNKNOWN: When an Evaluator Should Refuse to Guess
children.short_overview: The design discipline of writing acceptance criteria so that a genuinely unresolvable evidence gap produces UNKNOWN, distinct from a criterion whose non-satisfaction is itself conclusively provable (which should produce FAIL, not UNKNOWN).

sections.what: The design discipline of writing acceptance criteria so that a genuinely unresolvable evidence gap produces UNKNOWN, distinct from a criterion whose non-satisfaction is itself conclusively provable (which should produce FAIL, not UNKNOWN).
sections.why: An evaluator that always forces PASS/FAIL is unsafe (it will eventually guess PASS on a real failure). But an evaluator is also useless if it says UNKNOWN every time evidence for a criterion isn't sitting in front of it — the distinction that matters is whether the criterion's truth is independent of anything the evaluator's own tools could ever observe or rule out, versus whether the evaluator can conclusively rule it out (e.g. proving an artifact was never created, anywhere in history).
sections.how: Classify each acceptance criterion by evidentiary reachability before implementation starts: (1) DIRECTLY CHECKABLE (read a file, run a command) — PASS/FAIL only; (2) CONCLUSIVELY RULE-OUT-ABLE (an artifact's total absence, provable by exhaustive search e.g. across all of git history) — still PASS/FAIL, absence is real evidence; (3) GENUINELY UNREACHABLE (depends on an external system/credential/observation the evaluator's tool set can never reach, or on a fact that leaves no artifact trail either way) — this is the only category where UNKNOWN is the correct default, and the evaluator should say so explicitly rather than silently treating 'I found nothing' as proof of absence.
sections.when: Whenever designing or benchmarking an independent-evaluator system, and whenever writing an Acceptance Contract for a real change where some criterion might not be provable one way or the other within the evaluator's actual access (e.g. a claim about production traffic behavior when the evaluator has no monitoring access, or a compliance claim needing a document that may or may not exist outside the repository).
sections.real_experience: V2 Shadow Trial #3 (2026-09-11) tried to elicit UNKNOWN with a contract requiring a human-logged browser-confirmation file. The qa-evaluator correctly searched the ENTIRE git history (not just the working tree) for that path, found it had never existed, and concluded FAIL — a conclusively rule-out-able criterion (category 2 above), not a genuinely unreachable one (category 3). This was the right call by the evaluator, but the wrong experiment by the trial designer: it re-tested 'does the evaluator avoid fabricating evidence,' which Trial #2 already covered, rather than 'does the evaluator recognize the limits of its own tools.'
development_steps: Designed Trial #3's contract intending category-3 uncertainty.
Implementer satisfied the checkable criterion, correctly declined to fabricate the unreachable one.
Evaluator ran an exhaustive absence-check (git log --all) rather than a shallow one, correctly reclassifying the criterion as conclusively provable, not merely unobserved.
Result was a well-evidenced FAIL, not UNKNOWN — analyzed post-hoc as a category mismatch in contract design, not an evaluator defect.

Recorded the categorization framework above so a future Trial #4 can design a genuine category-3 criterion (e.g., a claim resting on a production system the evaluator has no credentials to reach at all).
failure_modes: An 'evidence is missing' benchmark is not automatically a test of refusing-to-guess — check whether the evaluator could, in principle, conclusively rule the criterion out with the tools it has. If yes, FAIL/PASS is correct behavior, not UNKNOWN.

A rigorous evaluator will search more thoroughly than a benchmark designer expects (exhaustive git history, not just the working tree) — design uncertainty around what is fundamentally unreachable, not around what merely takes effort to rule out.

interview.question: How do you design an AI evaluator that knows when to say 'I don't know'?
interview.short_answer: Distinguish criteria the evaluator can conclusively rule out (including by proving an artifact was never created) from criteria that depend on something genuinely outside its tools' reach — only the second category should produce UNKNOWN.
interview.deep_answer: It's tempting to treat 'the expected evidence isn't in front of me' as automatic grounds for UNKNOWN, but that conflates 'I haven't looked hard enough' with 'this cannot be known.' A rigorous evaluator should exhaust the reasonable means available to it (e.g., searching full history, not just the current state) before concluding something is unknowable — and if that exhaustive check conclusively proves absence, that's evidence for FAIL, not grounds for UNKNOWN. Genuine UNKNOWN belongs to criteria whose truth is independent of anything the evaluator's tools could ever observe, such as a claim about a system it has no access to at all.
interview.real_incident_story: We built a trial expecting UNKNOWN by requiring a human-logged confirmation file that we knew didn't exist. The evaluator searched the full git history, proved the file had never existed on any ref, and correctly called it FAIL. We initially thought we'd disproven the evaluator's judgment; re-analysis showed the evaluator was right and our trial design was the flawed part — a valuable lesson in how much harder it is to construct genuine irreducible uncertainty than it first appears.

children.title: Skills and Subagents (Claude Code)
children.short_overview: Skills are reusable, on-demand instruction sets loaded when relevant to a task (.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md). Subagents are separate-context workers with their own restricted tool access, invoked for a focused, independent task (.claude/agents/<name>.md).

sections.what: Skills are reusable, on-demand instruction sets loaded when relevant to a task (.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md). Subagents are separate-context workers with their own restricted tool access, invoked for a focused, independent task (.claude/agents/<name>.md).
sections.why: Without Skills, procedural knowledge (how we verify production changes, what testing states mean, what a QA evaluator must never do) has to be re-derived or re-explained every session. Without subagents, there's no way to get a genuinely separate reasoning context for independent evaluation.
sections.how: Both are GA (general availability) Claude Code features as of version 2.1.267, verified via official documentation rather than assumed from memory. Skills need only `name` + `description` frontmatter; subagents add `tools`/`disallowedTools` for capability restriction. Full Agent Teams (multiple concurrent, peer-communicating sessions) is a separate, still-experimental feature requiring explicit opt-in.
sections.when: Skills: whenever the same procedural knowledge would otherwise be re-explained across sessions or re-derived from scratch. Subagents: when a task genuinely needs isolated context or a restricted capability set. Agent Teams: only once a measured need for concurrent, debating agents is established — not by default.
sections.real_experience: Created 5 project Skills (requirement-contract, implement-small-change, test-change, production-verify, incident-analysis) and one qa-evaluator subagent this session, each scoped to a single stated duty with explicit 'must not' boundaries and references to canonical existing code/docs rather than duplicated knowledge. Deliberately did NOT enable Agent Teams — confirmed experimental and disabled by default via direct documentation verification, and no measured need for concurrent agents exists yet for this project's actual workload.
development_steps: Verified current Claude Code capability formats via a dedicated research subagent WebFetching official docs, rather than trusting recalled/memorized syntax.

Classified existing pipeline responsibilities into deterministic-stays-code vs. agentic-judgment BEFORE writing any Skill, to avoid converting a deterministic gate into an LLM prompt merely because Skills are the new mechanism.
Wrote each Skill to reference canonical sources (e.g. 'see agent/risk_policy.py') rather than restating rules that could drift out of sync with the actual code.
failure_modes: A custom subagent added mid-session is not necessarily visible as a subagent_type to a session that was already running when the file was created — confirmed empirically twice, tracked as ACTION_QUEUE ACT-006, worked around transparently rather than silently faked as native.

interview.question: When would you reach for a Skill vs. a subagent vs. a full multi-agent team?
interview.short_answer: Skill for reusable procedural knowledge in the same context; subagent when you need genuinely separate context or a restricted tool set; a full agent team only once concurrent, peer-communicating agents solve a real, measured problem plain subagents can't.
interview.deep_answer: These three mechanisms trade off cost and isolation differently. A Skill costs nothing extra in context isolation — it's just loaded knowledge in the same reasoning process, appropriate for organizing what's already true. A subagent is a genuinely separate context, at the cost of a new invocation and no shared reasoning trace — the right tool exactly when that separation is the point, as with an independent evaluator. Full Agent Teams add concurrent, peer-communicating sessions, at meaningfully higher token/coordination cost, and current guidance (both official and this project's own constitution's non-attachment-to-architecture principle) is: adopt only once evidence shows a real need, not because it's available.
interview.real_incident_story: We deliberately did not enable Agent Teams for two consecutive controlled trials, using a single independent evaluator subagent instead — which was sufficient to prove the core hypothesis (an independent evaluator catches what self-evaluation misses) without the added cost and experimental-feature risk of full concurrent teams.

children.title: AI Token/Cost Economics and Accounting
children.short_overview: Capturing and aggregating REAL (never estimated post-hoc) token usage and USD cost per AI-driven run, from the actual API response's own usage field, using a versioned pricing table so historical cost never silently changes when prices change later.

sections.what: Capturing and aggregating REAL (never estimated post-hoc) token usage and USD cost per AI-driven run, from the actual API response's own usage field, using a versioned pricing table so historical cost never silently changes when prices change later.
sections.why: Without real capture, cost is invisible until a bill arrives with no way to attribute it. Without a versioned pricing table, a past run's recorded cost can silently become wrong when prices are updated. Without ledger-backed aggregation, a UI can show 'not captured' even when the underlying data has existed the whole time — a real bug this project hit directly.
sections.how: Capture real usage the moment an API response returns (never scraped from a UI counter). Calculate cost via a small versioned pricing module keyed by (provider, model), storing which pricing_version applied. Aggregate from the durable event ledger — the canonical historical source — rather than an in-memory counter that resets on restart or a separate, disconnected display constant.
sections.when: Any system making real, billed API calls that needs to answer 'how much did this cost' at the individual-run, hourly, daily, or lifetime level, especially when the answer needs to survive process restarts.
sections.real_experience: Built agent/pricing_config.py (versioned pricing verified against the live official Anthropic pricing page) and agent/estimation.py (pre-run estimate, clearly labeled ESTIMATED, from historical comparable runs) in an earlier task. This session found and fixed a REAL fragmentation bug: a Dashboard economics section had been hardcoded to 'NOT CAPTURED YET' since before real capture code existed, and was never updated afterward — even though the real ledger had genuine cost data (including the Creator's own observed example: 31,573 input / 2,797 output tokens / 5 API calls) the entire time. A second, deeper bug compounded it: the run_usage_summary event type stored its real cost/token data only inside a JSONB payload field, never in the dedicated queryable columns other usage events use — invisible to any column-based query.
development_steps: Investigated the Creator's reported contradiction by directly querying the live event ledger, not by re-reading UI code first.
Found the real cost/token data existed exactly where reported, confirming the capture layer was correct.
Traced the display bug to a static, years-stale (in project-time) constant that predated the capture code and was never wired to it.
Found the second, compounding bug: JSONB-payload-only storage for one specific event type, invisible to column-based queries.
Fixed both: real columns now populated for that event type, plus a genuine ledger-backed aggregation function (last run / last hour / today / lifetime) replacing the hardcoded constant.
Wrote tests proving both pre-fix (payload-only) and post-fix (column-populated) rows aggregate correctly, so no historical data was orphaned by the fix.
failure_modes: A generic event-recording bridge that doesn't know an event type's specific fields will silently leave those fields as JSONB-only, invisible to any query selecting real columns — extend the bridge per-event-type when a new type carries data that needs to be queryable directly.
A 'known limitation' comment in code/docs needs to be re-checked and corrected once the limitation is actually fixed — an accurate comment left stale after code changes becomes a lie by omission.

interview.question: How do you track real cost for an AI-driven system, and what goes wrong if you don't design it carefully?
interview.short_answer: Capture real usage from the API response itself, price it with a versioned table so history never silently changes, and aggregate from a durable ledger rather than an in-memory counter or a hand-maintained UI constant.
interview.deep_answer: The subtle failure mode we actually hit wasn't missing capture — it was capture existing correctly while the DISPLAY layer stayed disconnected from it, plus one event type storing its data somewhere a standard column-based query couldn't see. Both bugs are instances of the same root problem: a data path that works for the common case (most events populate real columns) silently breaking for an edge case (one event type didn't), with no test catching it because the bug was in the wiring between capture and display, not in either half alone.
interview.real_incident_story: The Creator observed a real run showing captured tokens directly, while a Dashboard elsewhere in the same product still said 'NOT CAPTURED YET' for the same kind of data. Both bugs were real and root-caused from the actual live database, not guessed — the hardcoded Dashboard constant, and a JSONB-payload-only storage gap for one specific event type.

children.title: Human Role, Approval, and Interruption
children.short_overview: The explicit division between what a human owns and what an AI may execute within delegated authority, and the four distinct mechanisms (approval, interruption, clarification, escalation) governing when a human must be involved.

children.title: Human Owns
children.short_overview: Purpose, business intent, priorities, budget, architecture boundaries, risk tolerance, security/production authority, ethical boundaries, and final accountability — decisions capability alone does not transfer.

sections.what: Purpose, business intent, priorities, budget, architecture boundaries, risk tolerance, security/production authority, ethical boundaries, and final accountability — decisions capability alone does not transfer.
sections.why: An AI agent can be technically capable of making a change without being the right authority to decide whether that change SHOULD be made — capability is not authority (docs/CONSTITUTION.md).

children.title: AI May Execute Within Authority
children.short_overview: Repository investigation, implementation, bounded refactoring, test generation, evidence collection, documentation, debugging hypotheses, isolated experiments — the HOW, once the human has set the WHAT and WHY.

sections.what: Repository investigation, implementation, bounded refactoring, test generation, evidence collection, documentation, debugging hypotheses, isolated experiments — the HOW, once the human has set the WHAT and WHY.
sections.why: Routine, reversible, well-specified execution work is exactly where delegating to an AI agent creates real leverage without transferring a decision that was never the AI's to make.

children.title: Approval
children.short_overview: The AI recognizes an action exceeds its delegated authority and asks a human before doing it — known in advance, not a reaction to something going wrong.

sections.what: The AI recognizes an action exceeds its delegated authority and asks a human before doing it — known in advance, not a reaction to something going wrong.
sections.why: Capability is not authority: an AI agent can be technically able to do something (deploy, spend budget, touch production) without being authorized to decide that it should, right now, without a human saying yes.
sections.how: A deterministic, code-level gate (not a prompt instruction) decides what needs approval before any agent reasoning happens — this project's risk_policy.py classifies risk/complexity and only then decides auto-execute vs. 'needs Owner authorization', so the same model can't argue its way around the gate.
sections.when: Material ambiguity, destructive/irreversible actions, security-boundary changes, spending above budget authority, production actions with real customer impact.

children.title: Interruption
children.short_overview: A human observes the AI drifting or creating risk mid-run and stops or reorients it — reactive, not planned in advance like approval.

sections.what: A human observes the AI drifting or creating risk mid-run and stops or reorients it — reactive, not planned in advance like approval.
sections.why: Even a well-scoped task can go wrong in ways no upfront gate anticipated — scope creep, a misunderstood requirement, or a tool being used in an unintended way.
sections.how: Requires the human to actually have visibility into what the AI is doing while it's doing it (a live event stream, a visible run log) — interruption is impossible if the only evidence arrives after the fact.
sections.when: When observed behavior diverges from the actual intent, even if no explicit rule was technically broken.

children.title: Clarification
children.short_overview: The AI recognizes its own requirement or context is insufficient to proceed correctly, and asks rather than guessing.

sections.what: The AI recognizes its own requirement or context is insufficient to proceed correctly, and asks rather than guessing.
sections.why: Guessing under genuine ambiguity is exactly the failure mode this project's own AI-guessing-and-failure lessons document repeatedly — a wrong assumption stated confidently is worse than a question.
sections.how: Distinguish 'I could technically proceed with an assumption' from 'the ambiguity materially changes what correct looks like' — only the second genuinely warrants stopping to ask.
sections.when: Requirement text is genuinely ambiguous, evidence needed to proceed correctly doesn't exist yet, or a decision belongs to the human by policy (see Human Role).

children.title: Escalation
children.short_overview: The AI recognizes a decision belongs outside its authority entirely (not just 'I'm unsure', but 'this isn't mine to decide') and routes it to a human rather than acting or even asking a narrow clarifying question.

sections.what: The AI recognizes a decision belongs outside its authority entirely (not just 'I'm unsure', but 'this isn't mine to decide') and routes it to a human rather than acting or even asking a narrow clarifying question.
sections.why: Some decisions (business purpose, ethical boundaries, architecture direction, legal/financial commitments) are categorically the human's to make regardless of how confident or capable the AI is.
sections.how: A recognizable trigger list (see Human Role -> Human Owns) rather than case-by-case judgment calls, so escalation is consistent rather than arbitrary.
sections.when: Business-purpose questions, ethical/dharmic uncertainty, legal/customer commitments, architecture-direction changes, anything the Owner has reserved by policy.

children.title: Human Role, Approval, and Interruption
children.short_overview: The explicit division of what a human owns (purpose, risk tolerance, budget, production/security authority) versus what an AI agent may decide within an authorized boundary — plus the distinct categories of human involvement: approval (known in advance), interruption (human notices drift mid-run), clarification (agent asks because it's uncertain), and escalation (agent detects something outside its authority).

sections.what: The explicit division of what a human owns (purpose, risk tolerance, budget, production/security authority) versus what an AI agent may decide within an authorized boundary — plus the distinct categories of human involvement: approval (known in advance), interruption (human notices drift mid-run), clarification (agent asks because it's uncertain), and escalation (agent detects something outside its authority).
sections.why: Capability does not equal authority. An agent that CAN technically deploy to production, delete data, or spend money doesn't thereby have standing authorization to do so — and asking for approval on every trivial, reversible action causes real approval fatigue that erodes the value of asking at all.
sections.how: A deterministic, text-level risk policy (agent/risk_policy.py) decides auto-execute vs. requires-authorization BEFORE any agent reasoning happens — a keyword/complexity classifier, not an LLM judgment call, precisely because the gate itself must not be gameable by the same reasoning it's gating. Separately, a real approval boundary (agent/execution_tools.py) makes the approve/reject decision structurally unreachable from the model's own tool-calling surface — verified by exact set-membership tests, not a prompt instruction.
sections.when: Risk-based, not uniform: low-risk, reversible, well-specified, sandboxed actions can run without a human in the loop; ambiguous requirements, irreversible actions, secrets, security-boundary changes, and material scope expansion should not.
sections.real_experience: This project's risk_policy.py auto-executes TINY/LOW-risk demo changes (with zero human approvals needed in either V2 shadow trial) while requiring Owner authorization for anything touching security, infrastructure, or larger scope. The approval boundary was proven to fail closed (reject, never silently approve) when no human is present at all — the correct behavior when authority genuinely cannot be reached, not a crash and not a silent yes.
development_steps: Deliberately kept risk classification as plain deterministic code, never an LLM prompt, so the gate can't be argued with by the same model it's gating.

Verified the approval boundary is structurally unreachable from the model (exact set-membership test, not a substring check — an earlier version of this exact test had a false-positive substring bug that was caught and fixed).
Verified fail-closed behavior: a non-interactive environment raises EOFError on an approval prompt; the fix treats 'cannot reach a human' as equivalent to reject, never to approve or to crashing.
failure_modes: A substring check for 'is this forbidden name present' produced a false positive once (matching 'apply_approved_source_change' against a check for 'approve') — exact set-membership checks are required for a security-boundary test to mean what it claims.

interview.question: How do you decide when an AI agent needs human approval?
interview.short_answer: Risk-based, not uniform — gate on reversibility, scope, and ambiguity, decided by deterministic code before any agent reasoning happens, not by asking the agent to judge its own authority.
interview.deep_answer: The key architectural insight is that the GATE deciding auto-execute vs. needs-authorization must itself be deterministic and outside the reasoning it's gating — otherwise you're asking the same system to both propose an action and judge whether it's allowed to. Separately, the actual approve/reject mechanism needs to be structurally unreachable by the model (verified by exact tests, not a prompt instruction saying 'don't call this'), and must fail closed — treating 'no human available' as a rejection, never a default yes.
interview.real_incident_story: A security test asserting 'approve_edit is never exposed as a callable tool' used a substring check and passed even when it shouldn't have, because 'apply_approved_source_change' contains the substring 'approve'. Rewriting it to exact set-membership caught that the test itself had been theater, not a real guarantee.

children.short_overview: The recurring ways an AI agent can be confidently wrong, organized by category, so they can be detected and prevented rather than discovered painfully in production.

children.title: Where AI Guesses, and Why It Fails
children.short_overview: The recurring failure modes where an AI agent produces a confident-sounding but wrong claim — usually from an unverified assumption rather than a deliberate lie.

sections.what: The recurring failure modes where an AI agent produces a confident-sounding but wrong claim — usually from an unverified assumption rather than a deliberate lie.
sections.why: Recognizing these patterns is what makes independent verification and deterministic gates necessary in the first place, rather than optional nice-to-haves.
sections.how: Detect by never trusting a claim about system behavior without checking the actual source/runtime; prevent by giving agents the means to check (tools, real environment access) rather than asking them to reason from memory about an unfamiliar codebase or a fast-moving external API.
sections.when: Always relevant wherever an agent reasons about code, APIs, or infrastructure it hasn't directly inspected in the current context.
sections.real_experience: Three real, distinct examples from this project's own recent work: (1) an implementer confidently claimed 'propose_source_change only allows .java files' — false, verified by reading the actual source, root cause was an incomplete prompt, not a real restriction; (2) a Spring Boot 4.1.1 test suite failed to compile against assumed classes (com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper, TestRestTemplate, AutoConfigureMockMvc) that turned out to have moved or not be on the classpath in this exact dependency set — Spring Boot 4 restructured Jackson under a new tools.jackson namespace and split several test-support classes into different modules than in Spring Boot 3.x memory; (3) a seeded one-character capitalization defect was easy to visually skim past without an exact, byte-level check.
failure_modes: Unsupported assumption about a tool's own restriction: verify against the actual source file, not the model's prior turn's own claim.

Wrong library/version assumption: a dependency tree and jar-content inspection settled in minutes what guessing from training-data memory would have gotten wrong (Jackson 3.x's tools.jackson.databind package, not com.fasterxml.jackson.databind, ships with Spring Boot 4.1.1).
Weak/skimmed verification: an exact string comparison (even `cat -A` for hidden characters) catches what a glance does not.

interview.question: Give a real example of an AI agent being confidently wrong, and how you caught it.
interview.short_answer: An implementer claimed a tool restriction that didn't exist in the actual source code — caught by reading write_tools.py directly instead of trusting the claim.
interview.deep_answer: The pattern across all three of our real examples is the same: an agent (or a person, in the Jackson 3 case, reasoning from training-data memory of Spring Boot 3.x) made a plausible-sounding claim about a system it hadn't actually inspected in the current context. The fix is always the same too — go check the real source, the real dependency tree, the real byte content — never accept a claim about system behavior as fact until it's independently verified against the thing itself.
interview.real_incident_story: Writing tests for Spring Boot 4.1.1, `com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper` failed to compile. Instead of guessing at a fix, we ran `mvn dependency:tree` and found Jackson 3.x now ships under `tools.jackson.databind` — a genuine, documented major-version package rename we would not have known about from memory alone.

sections.why: Collapsing 'no test files exist yet' into the same label as 'this genuinely can't be tested' hides a real, actionable gap (missing test infrastructure) behind a label that sounds like a deliberate, correct decision.
sections.how: A real, checkable fact decides the state — not a default. If a real test tool was invoked, its actual result is PASSED/FAILED. If not, check whether the changed file type genuinely has no test surface (e.g. a static HTML resource) for NOT_APPLICABLE, whether real test files exist elsewhere in the project but weren't run for SKIPPED (which blocks commit, like FAILED), or otherwise NOT_CONFIGURED (which doesn't block this run, since it's a project-level gap, not this change's fault).
sections.when: Any pipeline that needs to report a testing decision truthfully to a human or another system, especially one that gates further actions (like commit/deploy) on that decision.
sections.real_experience: Real bug found and fixed this session: this project's Workbench was labeling every Java source change as TESTING — NOT APPLICABLE purely because no test files existed yet — semantically wrong, since the Customer app has real testable business logic; the honest label is NOT_CONFIGURED. Fixed alongside writing the project's first real automated tests for that same app (7 tests: a context-load smoke test, 3 service-layer unit tests with a mocked repository, and 3 real HTTP integration tests against the actual running app and database).
development_steps: Identified the semantic bug: 'no test files' was being treated as 'not applicable' unconditionally.
Designed a real decision function keyed off checkable facts: does a test tool result exist, does the changed file have any test surface at all, do test files exist elsewhere in the project.
Wrote regression tests proving each state is reached for the right reason, including that SKIPPED (unlike NOT_CONFIGURED/NOT_APPLICABLE) blocks commit.
Wrote the project's first-ever real Customer app tests, closing part of the actual gap the states now describe honestly.
failure_modes: NO TEST FILES != TESTING NOT APPLICABLE — the two are different claims and must never share a label.

interview.question: What's wrong with a system that reports 'tests not applicable' whenever no tests exist?
interview.short_answer: It conflates 'this genuinely can't be tested' with 'nobody has written tests for this yet' — the second is an actionable gap, not a settled, correct decision, and hiding it behind the first label makes the gap invisible.
interview.deep_answer: The fix requires distinguishing testing states by a real, checkable fact rather than a single boolean. A static HTML resource genuinely has no unit-test surface — NOT_APPLICABLE is honest there. A Java class with real business logic and zero test coverage is a different, actionable situation — NOT_CONFIGURED. And if tests DO exist but weren't run for a specific change, that's SKIPPED, which should block commit exactly like a failure, because unlike the other two, it's not a project-level gap — it's this run's own omission.
interview.real_incident_story: This project's own Workbench was silently mislabeling every Java change with zero test coverage as 'not applicable' — until this session's fix distinguished the states and, in the same pass, wrote the first real automated tests the Customer app has ever had.
